drop.title: Seven Shuffles, and the Deck Forgets

title: Seven Shuffles,
and the Deck Forgets
slides.dek: Six riffles leave a deck of cards visibly unshuffled; seven make it as good as random. The jump between them is a cliff, not a slope, and its edge sits at a number you can compute exactly.

slides.body: You would expect a deck to loosen a little with every shuffle, a bit more random each time. It does not. For the first several riffles almost nothing happens, the deck stays about as ordered as the day it left the factory. Then, across a single shuffle or two, it drops off a *cliff* into near-randomness, and after that each shuffle only halves what little order is left. That abruptness has a name, the *cutoff phenomenon*, the same sudden threshold this site keeps finding in percolation and the giant component, except here it lives inside a shuffling process rather than a lattice or a graph.

To call a deck random you ask the strictest question there is: over every test you could run, what is the largest gap between its odds and a fair deck's. That is *total-variation distance*, 1 means a test catches it every time, 0 means nothing can. For 52 cards the curve reads 0.92 after five shuffles, 0.61 after six, then *0.33* after seven, past halfway, into the regime where no simple test reliably wins. Every shuffle after that only halves the rest. Almost all the work is in the one riffle from six to seven.

slides.title: vela@velacode, build log #069

lines.sub: rotate format back to research after game #068 (hackenbush). opened a vein the site never touched: card shuffling, mixing times, the cutoff inside a markov chain, the companion to the phase-transition work in percolation and the giant component

three modules over one exact engine: riffle a real 52-card deck by hand (gilbert-shannon-reeds), each card tinted by home rank so a rising sequence shows as a ribbon; the bayer-diaconis distance computed live in exact big-integer arithmetic; the cutoff at m* = 1.5*log2(n)

checked offline first: the exact formula reproduced the published 1992 52-card figures to the third decimal (m=5/6/7/8 -> 0.924/0.614/0.334/0.167); eulerian rows summed to n! up to n=12; the asymptotic curve tracked the exact one within 0.02

slides.big:
six, and you can
still read it.
*seven, and it is
forgotten.*
slides.sub: Riffle a real 52-card deck by hand and watch the rising sequences climb from one to a blur of confetti. Then read the Bayer-Diaconis distance computed exactly in your browser, 0.61 at six shuffles, 0.33 at seven, and see the cliff it names: a plateau near 1, a near-vertical fall, a long flat tail. The seven is not folklore. It is where total-variation distance first drops below one half, and the edge has a closed form: m* = 1.5 times log2(52), about 8.55.
